analysis.one_liner: Raises federal fines on employers caught violating child labor laws.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise child labor penalties from a maximum of $11,000 to as much as $132,270 was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, an employer caught illegally employing a child can be fined at most $11,000 per violation, and up to $50,000 if the violation caused serious injury or death. This bill would raise those fines to at least $5,000 and up to $132,270 per violation, and up to $601,150 when a violation causes death or serious injury. It was introduced by a Democrat with a Republican original cosponsor, sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers who are illegally employed, especially in hazardous jobs, gain because larger fines give employers a stronger financial reason to follow the law. Employers that already comply also benefit, since violators would no longer be able to treat an $11,000 fine as a routine cost of doing business. Taxpayers and courts benefit from clearer, stronger deterrence instead of repeat violations.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the current maximum civil penalty of $11,000 for a child labor violation with a minimum of $5,000 and a maximum of $132,270. [S2] [S3]
When a child labor violation causes death or serious injury, the penalty range rises from a maximum of $50,000 to a minimum of $25,000 and a maximum of $601,150. [S2] [S3]
The new penalty ranges apply to violations occurring on or after enactment, so higher fines would immediately apply to new violations. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Employers who violate child labor laws, and the industries that rely on underage workers in hazardous or long-hour jobs, would bear the cost through much larger fines when caught. This includes agricultural operations, food processing and meatpacking plants, and staffing agencies that place minors in prohibited work.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers using underage or hazardous child labor

drawbacks.text: Higher fines do not increase detection. The bill raises penalties but adds no funding or staffing for the wage-and-hour inspectors who find violations, so a fine only deters employers who expect to be caught. [S2] [S3]
The bill sets a $5,000 minimum fine per violation, which can be a heavy penalty for a small business or a family farm with a first-time paperwork error, not just for serious exploitation. [S3]
The $132,270 and $601,150 caps are fixed numbers rather than indexed to inflation, so over time they would erode the same way the old $11,000 cap did. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go to children kept out of illegal or dangerous work, and the costs fall only on employers who break the law. The main honest objection is design, not direction: a larger fine deters nothing if an employer is unlikely to be inspected, so raising penalties without adding enforcement capacity limits how much this bill would accomplish. A fixed $5,000 minimum could also over-penalize minor first offenses by small employers. On balance it is a modest, well-aimed change that leaves the harder enforcement problem untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2023 and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which never held a hearing or markup on it, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 29, 2023 by Rep. Hillary Scholten with Rep. Nancy Mace as an original cosponsor. [S1] [S3]
The same day it was introduced, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce. [S1] [S5]
It attracted 7 cosponsors, 6 Democrats and 1 Republican. [S4]

The only recorded action after the referral was the sponsor's introductory remarks printed in the Congressional Record the next day; no hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate action ever followed before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025. [S5] [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who use underage or hazardous child labor are better off, because the maximum fine for a violation stays at $11,000 per violation and $50,000 for ones causing serious injury or death, which many large operations can absorb as a business cost. The committee leadership that never scheduled the bill also kept the status quo intact without needing to vote against it on the record.

for.name: Rep. Hillary Scholten
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor the day after referral. [S1] [S5]

for.name: Rep. Nancy Mace
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced. [S3]

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the committee held no hearing or markup and the bill never left committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was genuinely bipartisan but small: a Democratic sponsor with a Republican original cosponsor and 7 total cosponsors (6 D, 1 R), while the Republican-chaired committee that controlled its fate never took it up.

industries.industry: Employers using underage or hazardous child labor (agriculture, food processing, meatpacking, staffing agencies)
industries.note: These employers currently face a maximum $11,000 fine per violation, which can function as a manageable cost of using cheap underage labor. The bill would raise that to as much as $132,270, and to $601,150 when a child is seriously injured or killed, directly raising the price of exploiting young workers. [S2] [S3]

industries.industry: Law-abiding employers in the same industries
industries.note: Businesses that follow child labor rules would benefit from competitors no longer being able to undercut them with illegal underage labor backed by only an $11,000 worst-case fine. [S2]
